Reference guide · electricity and heat

Energy generation in Europe and Spain

The goal of this website is to introduce the different technologies used to generate electricity in Europe and Spain, so that they can be understood and compared. Three of them (solar thermal, aerothermal and hydrothermal) mainly produce heat rather than electricity; they are included because they are key renewable technologies for buildings and industry.

Each technology has its own section, organised in the same order. It starts with what the technology is and the physical principle behind it, followed by an animated demonstration that shows step by step how it works. It then explains how and where the technology is used, and how its use has changed over the years in the EU and in Spain. Next come its main types, with what they have in common and what sets them apart, and the state of the art: current records, new designs and open challenges. The economics part covers investment cost (CAPEX), operating cost (OPEX) and the cost per unit of energy (LCOE). Finally, the operation part shows how much energy the technology produces and how many hours a year it runs. Every figure comes from a public source, cited under each chart. A separate Fundamentals page explains the power cycles and how a turbine's rotation becomes electricity on the grid, and an Energy storage page compares electrical and thermal storage.

1 · The current situation

Where Europe and Spain stand

In 2025 almost half of the EU's electricity (47.7%) came from renewable sources. Nuclear is still the largest single source (23.3%), followed by wind (17.1%) and gas (16.7%). Solar has grown faster than anything else: it overtook coal in 2024 and hydropower in 2025, while coal fell from 30.5% of EU generation in 2000 to 9.2%. Fossil fuels together still produced about 29% of EU electricity.

Spain is further ahead in renewables (55.9%). Solar, wind and gas each produced around a fifth of its electricity in 2025, with nuclear close behind (18.8%), and coal has practically disappeared (0.3%). Gas generation rose in 2025, partly because, after the April blackout, the grid operator scheduled more gas plants to keep the system stable.

Shares computed from Ember Yearly Electricity Data (2026 release). Ember's solar figure includes an estimate of rooftop output; on the grid-only count used by Red Eléctrica, wind was Spain's largest source in 2025.

1 · Operation

How many hours a year each source runs

Equivalent full-load hours: the hours a plant would need at full power to produce its actual annual output. A year has 8,760 hours. The value reflects the resource (sun, wind, water) and also how the market dispatches each plant.

1 · Economics

What a kilowatt-hour costs to produce

The levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) spreads all lifetime costs (construction, operation, fuel, financing) over all lifetime output. The chart compares the global average for plants that started operating in 2024. Each technology section compares its own cost with fossil fuels.

2 · Problems

The main energy problems

Europe and Spain share some problems and differ on others. Each card is tagged by scope and by the technologies it affects.

EUnon-renewables

Imported fuel and price shocks

Gas set many of Europe's electricity prices during the 2022 crisis. In 2025 the EU still paid about €32 billion for gas imported to generate power (Ember). A new regulation, (EU) 2026/261, bans Russian gas imports in stages, ending with long-term contracts in 2027.

EUboth

Grids that lag behind generation

The Commission's Grid Action Plan estimates €584 billion of grid investment this decade. Reinforcing a line takes 4–10 years to permit, and about 40% of distribution grids are more than 40 years old.

EUrenewables

Dependence on China for equipment

China holds more than 80% of every stage of PV manufacturing (IEA). It is also the main source of the rare earths used in permanent-magnet wind generators. The Critical Raw Materials Act (2024) sets 2030 benchmarks: 10% EU extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling and no more than 65% from any single country.

Spainrenewables

Too much solar at midday

Spain had 556 hours of negative wholesale prices in 2025. In spring 2025 its solar plants earned only 54% of the average price, against 83% in spring 2023 (Modo Energy). More storage and demand are needed to use that energy.

Spainboth

A saturated grid and an "energy island"

Utilities report 83.4% of distribution nodes as saturated (Aelec, 2025). The link with France is only 2.8 GW, about 2.8% of installed capacity, against an EU target of 15% for 2030 (IEA). The Bay of Biscay link will raise it to 5 GW around 2027–2028.

Spainnon-renewables

Security of supply as nuclear closes

The 2019 calendar closes all seven reactors by 2035. In August 2026 the government extended Almaraz to June 2030. Combined-cycle gas plants run few hours but are still needed for voltage control and backup (see the blackout below).

Sources: Ember EER 2026; European Parliament, Regulation 2026/261; EU Grid Action Plan; IEA; EPRS, CRM Act; pv magazine (ENTSO-E data); Modo Energy; Endesa (Aelec maps); IEA, Spain; REE, Biscay link.

3 · Spain's electricity market

How the price of electricity is set

Electricity in Spain is sold in a daily auction where the most expensive plant needed sets the price for everyone. This explains why gas prices drive electricity bills, and why Spain and Portugal capped the gas price in 2022.

How the market works, the merit-order simulator and the Iberian exception

Every day, generators in Spain and Portugal send offers to the market operator OMIE for the next day: how much energy they can produce and at what minimum price. Buyers send bids too. The market sorts the offers from cheapest to most expensive (the "merit order") and accepts them until demand is covered. Since October 2025 this is done for every 15-minute period.

All accepted generators receive the same price: the offer of the last, most expensive plant needed. This is called marginal pricing. Solar, wind and nuclear offer close to zero because they have almost no fuel cost. When demand is high or there is little sun and wind, a gas plant is needed, and its fuel and CO₂ cost then set the price for everyone.

Afterwards Red Eléctrica (REE) adjusts the schedule for grid security ("technical constraints") and buys balancing services. Those costs are added to the bill on top of the market price.

The "Iberian exception" (2022–2023)

Royal Decree-law 10/2022

In 2022 gas prices soared and, through marginal pricing, so did electricity. Spain and Portugal obtained EU approval to cap the gas price used by power plants. From 15 June 2022 gas plants received a subsidy covering the difference between the market gas price and a cap of €40/MWh, rising by €5 a month to €70.

Gas plants could then offer lower prices, which lowered the marginal price for all electricity. The subsidy was paid by the buyers who benefited from the lower price. An extension set a new path from €55 to €65/MWh, and the mechanism ended on 31 December 2023. It had stopped having an effect after 26 February 2023, when gas fell below the cap.

Sources: Cuatrecasas; Maldita; Cuatrecasas (extension).

Other parts of the system

Beyond the day-ahead auction
  • Intraday markets let players correct their positions closer to real time.
  • Technical constraints and balancing (REE) keep voltage and frequency in range. After the 2025 blackout their cost rose sharply.
  • Capacity mechanism: approved by the European Commission in 2026, worth about €9 billion over 2026–2036, it pays plants, storage and demand response to be available.
  • Regulated tariff (PVPC): household price linked partly to the wholesale market.

Sources: ESS News; PwC.

4 · The 2025 Iberian blackout

28 April 2025, 12:33

At 12:33 CEST on 28 April 2025 mainland Spain and Portugal lost all electricity supply, the first event of its kind in Continental Europe according to ENTSO-E.

Timeline, causes and what changed afterwards

What happened

According to the official reports
  1. Before

    Oscillations in the grid in the half hour before. REE had scheduled 10 synchronous plants for voltage control, the lowest number of the year.

  2. 12:33

    Voltage rose fast. About 727 MW of solar PV and CSP tripped in Badajoz, then 928 MW more in about 2 seconds; total losses exceeded 2.5 GW, with voltages above 435 kV.

  3. Cascade

    Each disconnection raised the voltage further and more plants tripped, until the Iberian system separated from Europe and collapsed.

  4. Restart

    Hydropower plants able to start without external power ("black start") and the links with France and Morocco energised the grid again during the afternoon and night.

Causes and changes

Not a lack of inertia, but of voltage control
  • ENTSO-E final report (March 2026): fast voltage increases and cascading disconnections, with gaps in voltage and reactive power control. Some conventional units delivered less reactive power than required; many renewable plants ran at a fixed power factor and did not help.
  • Spanish government (June 2025): a multifactorial origin and insufficient voltage control capacity. A cyberattack was ruled out.
  • REE: the event "was not caused by an inertia problem".
  • Changes: renewables can now control voltage (new operating procedure 7.4, extended in 2026 to plants of 1 MW and over); eight synchronous condensers approved for the mainland; a stricter "reinforced operation" with more gas plants, costing €516 million from May to December 2025 (REE).

Sources: ENTSO-E; pv magazine (summary of the final report); MITECO; REE; CNMC; MITECO (grid measures); Energías Renovables (REE cost).

5 · The future

Where Europe and Spain are heading

EU targets

European Climate Law and Renewable Energy Directive
  • Net greenhouse gas emissions 55% below 1990 by 2030, and climate neutrality by 2050.
  • At least 42.5% renewables in final energy by 2030 (RED III), with faster permits in "acceleration areas".
  • Phase-out of Russian gas by 2027 and of coal in most member states before 2040.

Spain's plan (PNIEC 2023–2030)

Approved September 2024
  • 81% renewable electricity and 48% renewables in final energy by 2030.
  • Emissions 32% below 1990; energy dependence from 73% (2019) to 50%.
  • 12 GW of electrolysers for renewable hydrogen; €308 billion of investment, 82% private.

Source: MITECO (Sep 2024).

The challenges ahead

bothEU + Spain

Stability with fewer turbines spinning

Inverter-based plants do not add inertia or, unless required, voltage support. ENTSO-E recommends keeping system inertia of at least 2 MWs/MVA for more than half the year by 2035. The tools are grid-forming inverters, batteries and synchronous condensers.

renewablesEU + Spain

Storage and flexibility

Europe installed 36 GWh of batteries in 2025, passing 100 GWh in total (SolarPower Europe). Spain must grow from 3.4 GW of storage to 22.5 GW by 2030; pumped hydro calls and the capacity mechanism support this.

bothSpain

Grids and interconnections

Spain's 2025–2030 transmission plan grew from €13.6 billion (October 2025 proposal) to more than €17 billion after public consultation, and is still pending approval.

bothmaterials

Materials at the limit

Ultra-supercritical boilers need P92 steel up to about 620 °C and nickel alloys above about 675 °C. Gas turbine blades rely on ceramic coatings in gas near 2,000 °C. Molten salt corrodes CSP pipes at 565 °C, silica scales geothermal wells, chlorine attacks biomass boilers, and stress-corrosion cracking stopped 16 French reactors in 2022.

renewablesEU

End of life and recycling

About 25,000 t of wind blades a year reach end of life by 2025 and 52,000 t by 2030 (WindEurope). PV modules fall under the WEEE Directive (85% recovery). Silver use per PV cell keeps falling.

non-renewablesEU + Spain

Carbon, ageing plants and waste

The EU carbon price averaged €74/t in 2025. Europe's reactors average 36.7 years (GRS, including non-EU). Spain's 7th radioactive waste plan (2023) replaces the central store with seven on-site stores, at an estimated €20.2 billion.

Sources: Energy Storage Europe (ENTSO-E recommendation); SolarPower Europe; Energías Renovables; EPRI/DOE; DLR; MDPI Energies; WNN; WindEurope; IEA-PVPS; GRS; MITECO.

Units and terms

How to read the numbers

GW, GWe, GWth
Installed capacity. GWe is electrical output; GWth is thermal output, used for heating technologies. 1 GW = 1,000 MW.
TWh
Energy produced over a period. 1 TWh = 1,000 GWh = 10⁹ kWh.
Equivalent full-load hours (h)
Annual generation ÷ installed capacity. Maximum 8,760 h in a non-leap year.
Capacity factor (%)
Equivalent hours ÷ 8,760. 2,000 h ≈ 22.8%.
CAPEX
Total installed cost of building the plant, per kW of capacity.
OPEX
Operating costs. Fixed O&M is charged per kW per year; variable O&M and fuel per MWh produced.
LCOE
Discounted lifetime costs ÷ discounted lifetime generation, in USD/MWh or €/MWh.
WACC
Weighted average cost of capital: the discount rate used in the LCOE. IRENA's 2024 assumptions range from 3.8% (Europe) to 12% (Africa).
Dispatchable
Output can be scheduled on demand, as with fuel-based plants or solar plants with thermal storage.
Merit order
Generation offers sorted from cheapest to most expensive; the market accepts them in that order until demand is covered.
Marginal price
The offer of the last, most expensive plant needed. In the day-ahead market every accepted generator is paid this price.
Inertia (H) and RoCoF
Kinetic energy stored in spinning generators, in seconds of rated output. It limits the rate of change of frequency (RoCoF, Hz/s) after a disturbance.
Grid-following / grid-forming
Inverters that follow an existing grid voltage, or that create their own voltage like a synchronous generator.
COP / SCOP
Heat delivered ÷ electricity used by a heat pump, at one operating point (COP) or averaged over the heating season (SCOP).
Wp (watt-peak)
PV module power at standard test conditions: 1,000 W/m², 25 °C cell temperature, AM1.5 spectrum.
Solar · electricity

Solar photovoltaics

Semiconductor devices that turn sunlight directly into electricity, with no moving parts and no heat cycle. PV was the fastest-growing power source in both the EU and Spain over the last decade.

1 · Definition

What photovoltaics is

A photovoltaic cell is a semiconductor junction. When a photon with enough energy is absorbed, it frees an electron. The electric field built into the p–n junction separates electrons from the holes they leave behind, and the result is a direct current. Cells are wired into modules, modules into strings, and an inverter converts the direct current into alternating current at grid frequency.

Output follows the irradiance on the module surface. A plant produces nothing at night, less in winter and under cloud, and slightly less when cells are hot. Module power is therefore quoted in watts-peak (Wp), measured at standard test conditions (1,000 W/m², 25 °C, AM1.5 spectrum), and not under real outdoor conditions.

Main components

Modules · mounting structure (fixed tilt or single-axis tracker) · inverters (central, string or micro) · transformer and grid connection · monitoring. Rooftop systems add a bidirectional meter and, optionally, a battery.

How it differs from solar thermal and CSP

PV converts light into electricity directly. Solar thermal collectors turn sunlight into heat for hot water or space heating. CSP concentrates sunlight to drive a steam turbine and can store the heat. Only CSP has a thermodynamic cycle.

2 · Uses

How PV is deployed

Utility-scale plants

Ground-mounted plants of tens to hundreds of MW that sell into the wholesale market or through long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs). In Spain they are usually built on single-axis trackers that follow the sun from east to west. In 2025 utility-scale plants were more than half of new EU capacity for the first time.

Self-consumption

Rooftop systems on homes, businesses and factories that cover part of the building's own demand and export any surplus. Spain's Royal Decree 244/2019 allows individual and shared (collective) self-consumption, with or without compensation for surplus energy.

Off-grid systems

Isolated installations with batteries, used for farms, mountain huts or telecom sites without a grid connection. A small segment, but the only one that grew strongly in Spain in 2025.

Niche formats

Floating PV on reservoirs, agrivoltaics that share land with crops or grazing, and building-integrated PV (BIPV) that replaces façade or roof materials.

3 · Evolution

Twenty-five years of growth

Compare the EU and Spain on the same chart. Spain started early with a feed-in tariff boom in 2008, stalled for most of the 2010s, and then grew faster than the EU average from 2019.

Spain: the policy timeline behind the curve

Main regulatory changes
  1. 2007

    Royal Decree 661/2007 sets feed-in tariffs. Solar capacity jumps from 0.5 GW to 3.5 GW in 2008.

  2. 2012

    Royal Decree-law 1/2012 suspends economic incentives for new renewable plants. Growth almost stops.

  3. 2013–14

    Royal Decree-law 9/2013 and Royal Decree 413/2014 replace tariffs with a "reasonable return" regime, applied retroactively to existing plants.

  4. 2015

    Royal Decree 900/2015 charges self-consumers a backup toll, widely called the "sun tax".

  5. 2017

    Technology-neutral auctions award about 3.9 GW to PV, the first large wave of the new boom.

  6. 2018–19

    Royal Decree-law 15/2018 removes the toll. Royal Decree 244/2019 opens shared self-consumption and surplus compensation.

  7. 2025

    8.8 GW of new grid PV, about 88% of all renewable capacity added in Spain that year (REE).

Sources: Boletín Oficial del Estado (decree texts); capacity from Ember; 2025 additions from REE, Las renovables en el sistema eléctrico español 2025.

EU: milestones

From marginal to the third-largest source
  1. 2010

    Solar produces 23.5 TWh, 0.8% of EU electricity.

  2. 2023

    Solar generation passes lignite (254 vs 179 TWh).

  3. 2024

    Solar passes coal of all kinds for the first time (307 vs 272 TWh).

  4. 2025

    366 TWh, a 13.1% share. Wind and solar together (30%) exceed all fossil generation (29%) for the first time.

  5. 2025

    Installations fall 0.7% to 65.1 GW, the first decline since 2016. SolarPower Europe's central scenario is 718 GW by 2030, short of the 750 GW target.

Sources: Ember Yearly Electricity Data; Ember, European Electricity Review 2026; SolarPower Europe (Dec 2025).

4 · Types

Cell technologies

All PV technologies share the same principle: a semiconductor junction that delivers direct current, rated in Wp at standard test conditions and connected through the same kind of inverters and mounting structures. They differ in the absorber material, the manufacturing process, efficiency, cost and maturity.

p-typedeclining

PERC

Passivated Emitter and Rear Cell. A dielectric layer on the rear surface reduces electron losses. PERC was the mass-market standard of the late 2010s and is now losing share to n-type cells.

n-typemarket leader 2025

TOPCon

Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact. An ultra-thin oxide plus a doped polysilicon layer forms the rear contact. Existing PERC lines can be upgraded to make it, which explains its fast adoption. It led global production in 2025.

n-typegrowing

Heterojunction (HJT)

A crystalline wafer between thin amorphous-silicon layers, made in a low-temperature process. Very high voltage, but more silver per watt: about 12 mg/W, against 10 mg/W for bifacial TOPCon.

n-typegrowing

Back contact (IBC, HPBC, ABC)

All metal contacts sit on the rear, so nothing shades the front surface. Back-contact modules held the top commercial efficiency ranks at the end of 2025, and the cell technology holds the silicon record.

commercial

Cadmium telluride (CdTe)

A layer a few micrometres thick deposited directly on glass. It is the main commercial thin film, used mostly in large utility plants. It needs much less semiconductor material and energy to make than silicon wafers.

niche

CIGS and amorphous silicon

Copper-indium-gallium-selenide and amorphous silicon can be deposited on flexible substrates, which suits lightweight and integrated products. Their market share is small.

Market position

Crystalline silicon makes up about 98% of global PV production (ITRPV, 2025), so thin film and all other technologies together account for roughly 2%.

research

Perovskite single junction

Metal-halide perovskites absorb light strongly and can be processed at low temperature. Long-term stability under heat, moisture and light is the main barrier to commercial use.

pilot lines

Perovskite-on-silicon tandem

A perovskite top cell captures the blue part of the spectrum and a silicon bottom cell the red. This lets the stack exceed the practical limit of single-junction silicon, about 29.4%. The industry roadmap ITRPV expects mass production after 2027.

5 · State of the art

Where the technology stands in 2026

n-type has taken over

n-type wafers reached about 82% of the market in 2025, and TOPCon kept the lead among cell types. Global module shipments were about 706 GW. (ITRPV 2026)

Records keep moving

Silicon cells reached 27.81% in 2025, close to the theoretical limit of about 29.4%. Perovskite–silicon tandems reached 35.5% in July 2026, and 33% on a large 260.9 cm² cell.

Less silver, larger factories

Silver use fell about 20% in 2025 to roughly 7,244 t, still about 21% of world silver output. The roadmap expects about 6.3 mg/W for TOPCon by the mid-2030s, and factories of 5 GW or more per year increasingly dominate.

Prices turned up

Average spot prices for crystalline modules rose about 9% by end-2025 after steep falls in 2023–24. The long-run learning rate since 1976 is about 26%: each doubling of cumulative volume cut module prices by about a quarter.

Value at midday is falling

With so much PV producing at the same hours, Spanish solar plants earned 54% of the average wholesale price in spring 2025, down from 83% in spring 2023. Curtailment also set records in spring 2025. (Modo Energy)

Hybrid plants with batteries

Utility battery storage cost fell 93% between 2010 and 2024, to USD 192/kWh (IRENA). Pairing PV with storage shifts midday output into the evening peak.

Price vs fossil fuels

Half the cost of a new fossil plant

A new solar plant produces electricity at about half the cost of a new coal or gas plant (global averages). Solar only produces in daylight, so if storage or backup is added the gap narrows.

Spain's irradiance gives each solar kW far more output than the EU average. Spanish hours peaked in 2017 and have fallen since, most sharply in 2025.

Solar · heat

Solar thermal

Collectors that absorb sunlight and pass the heat to water, a glycol mix or air. It is the oldest and simplest way to use solar energy in buildings, and is growing in industry and district heating.

HeatHot water, space heating, process heatThermal storage built in
544GWthSolar thermal capacity in operation worldwideIEA SHC · 2024
443TWhHeat produced worldwide in one yearIEA SHC · 2024
43.6GWthCumulative capacity in EuropeSolar Heat Europe · 2024
3.67GWthCapacity in Spain, 5.2 million m² of collectorsASIT · 2024
1 · Definition

What solar thermal is

A solar thermal collector is a dark absorber plate or tube that turns solar radiation into heat. A fluid flowing through it carries the heat to a storage tank or straight to its use. Glazing and vacuum insulation reduce the losses back to the air, so the collector type depends on the temperature needed.

Systems either circulate by natural convection (thermosiphon, with the tank above the collector, common in southern Europe) or with a pump and controller (forced circulation). Collector capacity is usually reported in thermal watts: the sector converts collector area at 0.7 kWth per m², so 85,000 m² equals 59.5 MWth.

Main components

Collectors · hot-water storage tank · pump and differential controller (forced systems) · heat exchanger · backup heater (boiler or heat pump) for cloudy periods.

Difference from PV and CSP

Solar thermal delivers heat, not electricity, and usually works below 100 °C. PV makes electricity directly. CSP also concentrates sunlight into heat, but at several hundred degrees, to drive a turbine.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Where the heat goes

Domestic hot water

The classic use on homes and apartment blocks. In Spain, the 2006 Building Technical Code (CTE, HE4) required a minimum solar share of hot water in new buildings. The 2019 revision allows that share to come from other renewables, such as heat pumps.

Space heating and pools

"Combi" systems supply both hot water and heating. Unglazed collectors heat swimming pools cheaply in summer.

Solar district heating

Large collector fields feed city heating networks, often with seasonal pit storage. 346 towns and cities worldwide use solar district heating; ten new systems (74 MW) started in 2024.

Industrial process heat (SHIP)

Food, drinks, chemicals and textiles need heat between 30 °C and 400 °C. At least 106 new SHIP plants (120 MWth) started worldwide in 2024, 28% more than in 2023.

3 · Evolution

A market that peaked in 2008

Spain's market grew fast after the 2006 building code, peaked with the housing boom in 2008, and fell with construction. 2024 was the weakest year in two decades. Europe's market has also shrunk since 2008, while cumulative capacity keeps rising slowly because collectors last for decades.

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 1891

    Clarence Kemp patents the “Climax”, the first commercial solar water heater (Baltimore, US).

  2. 2006

    Spain's Technical Building Code (CTE) makes solar hot water compulsory in new and refurbished buildings.

  3. 2008

    Spanish collector sales peak at about 465,000 m² a year.

  4. 2024

    Groningen (Netherlands) installs 48,800 m² of collectors for district heating.

Sources: Solar water heating; ASIT and Solar Heat Europe (see Sources).

4 · Types

Collector families

All collectors share the same chain: absorb radiation, transfer heat to a fluid, store it. They differ in how well they are insulated, which sets the temperature they can reach and the cost per m².

low temperature

Unglazed

Plastic or metal absorbers with no cover. Cheap and efficient close to air temperature, so they suit swimming pools.

most common in Europe

Flat plate (glazed)

An insulated box with a selective absorber under a glass cover. The standard choice for domestic hot water in Europe.

higher temperature

Evacuated tube

Each absorber sits inside a glass tube with a vacuum, which cuts heat losses. Better in cold weather and at higher temperatures; dominant in China.

niche

Air collectors

Heat air directly for ventilation, drying crops or preheating process air.

100–400 °C

Parabolic trough, linear Fresnel, Scheffler

Mirrors focus direct sunlight on a receiver to make steam or hot oil for industry. Worldwide, 75 SHIP systems with parabolic troughs add up to 482 MWth, against 196 MWth from 331 flat-plate systems.

Relation to CSP

The same optics as concentrated solar power, used for heat instead of electricity and at a smaller scale.

growing

PVT collectors

A PV module with a heat exchanger behind it, producing electricity and heat from the same area. Cooling the cells also raises their electrical efficiency. A record 46 manufacturers reported sales in 2024, and Spain was one of the three leading markets with Germany and the Netherlands.

5 · State of the art

Where the technology is heading

Large district systems

Groningen (Netherlands, 2024) installed 48,800 m² for district heating. In Bracht, 11,637 m² of collectors with a 26,600 m³ seasonal pit store cover 75–80% of a 100% renewable network.

Industry is the growth market

1,315 SHIP systems were operating worldwide at the end of 2024. Plant sizes have grown from about 2 MWth to more than 30 MWth.

Shrinking rooftop market

Global additions fell 14% in 2024, to 17.8 GWth. In homes, solar thermal competes with PV plus heat pumps for the same roof.

6 · Economics

Costs

Solar thermal has no fuel cost, so almost all its cost is the upfront investment (collectors, tank, installation) spread over the system's operating life. Running costs are small: pump electricity and periodic checks of fluid and valves.

The Spanish association ASIT quotes solar process heat for industry at roughly €20–30 per MWh. That is an industry estimate, not an independent survey. This guide has not found a recent, free, EU-wide dataset of installed costs per m² for residential systems, so it does not publish one.

Price vs fossil fuels

Solar heat against gas heat

For industry, solar process heat costs about €20–30 per MWh according to ASIT, against about €57/MWh for heat from a gas boiler at 2025 wholesale gas and CO₂ prices. Households pay retail gas prices, which are higher.

7 · Operation

Heat produced per unit of capacity

For heat, the equivalent of "hours of generation" is the annual heat yield per kWth of collector. Dividing the world's 2024 heat output by capacity in operation gives the global average.

≈814kWh/kWthGlobal average annual yield, the same as about 814 full-load hours443 TWh ÷ 544 GWth · IEA SHC 2024
153.5Mt CO₂eEmissions avoided worldwide in a yearIEA SHC · 2024

Yield depends on climate, collector type and the temperature the user needs. Southern locations and low-temperature uses achieve more than the global average.

Solar · electricity

Concentrated solar power

Mirrors focus sunlight to produce high-temperature heat, which drives a steam turbine. Because heat is cheaper to store than electricity, CSP plants with molten-salt tanks can keep generating after sunset. Spain has the largest fleet in the world.

ElectricityDispatchable with storageNeeds direct sunlight
2.3GWCSP capacity in Spain, the largest in the worldREN21 · 2024
7.2GWCSP capacity worldwideREN21 · 2024
3,682GWhSpanish CSP generation, 1.4% of the mixREE · 2025
0.092$/kWhGlobal average LCOE of new plants, down 77% since 2010IRENA · 2024
1 · Definition

What CSP is

A CSP plant has three blocks. The solar field (mirrors that track the sun) concentrates direct sunlight onto a receiver. A heat transfer fluid, which can be synthetic oil, molten salt or water/steam, carries the heat away. A conventional power block, a Rankine steam cycle with a turbine, condenser and cooling system, converts that heat into electricity.

Mirrors can only focus the direct beam of sunlight, not the diffuse light from a cloudy sky. CSP therefore needs clear, dry climates with high direct normal irradiance (DNI), such as southern Spain, North Africa, the Middle East, Chile or western China.

The storage advantage

Part of the daytime heat is stored in tanks of molten salt and used to run the turbine in the evening. Gemasolar, near Seville, was the first commercial solar plant able to supply power around the clock, with 15 hours of storage.

What it shares with thermal plants

The power block is the same Rankine cycle studied for coal, biomass or nuclear plants. Only the heat source changes: mirrors instead of a boiler or reactor.

2 · Uses

How CSP is deployed

Spanish 50 MW plants

Most Spanish plants have exactly 50 MW because the 2007 tariff regime (Royal Decree 661/2007) was limited to plants of up to 50 MW.

Storage plants

About 20 of Spain's 50 plants have molten-salt storage, typically 7.5 hours (for example Andasol 1–3, 50 MW each). Thermal and electrical storage are compared on the Energy storage page.

Hybrid plants

The other Spanish plants keep a backup burner (gas or biomass) to stabilise output. In China, new "CSP+" projects pair a tower with large PV and wind farms and act as a storage and peak-shaving resource.

Process heat

The same concentrating optics supply steam to industry. That use is covered under Solar thermal.

3 · Evolution

Built in six years, then frozen

Spain: timeline

From the first commercial tower to today
  1. 2007

    PS10 (11 MW, Sanlúcar la Mayor) opens. It was the world's first commercial central-tower plant: 624 heliostats and a 115 m tower.

  2. 2007–13

    Feed-in tariffs under Royal Decree 661/2007 drive the construction of about 50 plants, around 2.3 GW.

  3. 2011

    Gemasolar (19.9 MW, more than 2,600 heliostats, 15 h of molten-salt storage) is inaugurated in Seville.

  4. 2012–14

    The 2012 moratorium and the retroactive reform stop new projects. No commercial plant has been added since.

  5. 2014

    Generation reaches 4,959 GWh, about 2% of demand.

  6. 2022

    The first auction reserved for CSP (220 MW) is declared void: all bids were above the reserve price.

  7. 2025

    3,682 GWh, 10.8% less than in 2024.

Where it is

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 1913

    Frank Shuman's parabolic trough plant at Maadi (Egypt) pumps irrigation water.

  2. 1984

    The first SEGS trough plant opens in California; the nine SEGS plants reach 354 MW by 1990.

  3. 2007

    PS10 (Seville), the world's first commercial solar tower.

    Andasol 1 (Granada), Europe's first trough plant with molten-salt storage, enters operation.

  6. 2013

    Spain completes its fleet of about 2.3 GW, still the largest in the world.

Sources: Concentrated solar power; PS10; Gemasolar.

4 · Types

Four ways to concentrate sunlight

Every CSP type uses mirrors, a receiver and a heat engine. They differ in the geometry of the mirrors: line-focus systems concentrate onto a tube, point-focus systems onto a single receiver, which reaches higher temperatures and cycle efficiencies.

most of Spain's fleet

Parabolic trough

Rows of curved mirrors track the sun on one axis and focus it on a receiver tube carrying thermal oil. The oil limits operation to about 400 °C. It is the most proven design; Andasol 1–3 are examples.

simpler, lower temperature

Linear Fresnel

Flat mirror strips near the ground focus onto a fixed receiver above them. Cheaper structures and less land, but lower optical efficiency. Spain has Fresnel plants in Murcia.

preferred for new plants

Central tower

A field of heliostats focuses on a receiver at the top of a tower. Molten salt can be used both as heat transfer fluid and as storage, with receiver temperatures above 500 °C (Gemasolar). Most of China's new CSP+ projects use 100 MW towers.

demonstration

Parabolic dish

A dish focuses on a Stirling engine at its focal point. The highest concentration, but each unit is small (kW scale) and there is no storage, so it has not reached commercial scale.

5 · State of the art

Where CSP stands

China leads new construction

About 8.1 GW was in development, construction or commissioning at the end of 2024, including 3.3 GW under construction. No new plant broke ground outside China in 2024.

Longer storage

New projects store 8 to 16 hours of heat: Yumen (China) 8 h, Zabuye (Tibet) 16 h plus a battery, and Italy's CSP 3 Bilancia 16 h.

Costs fell sharply

The global LCOE fell 46% in 2024 alone and 77% since 2010. IRENA attributes the long-term fall to longer storage, lower O&M costs and better use of capacity in high-DNI regions such as China and South Africa.

6 · Economics

CAPEX, LCOE and capacity factor

CAPEX per kW depends heavily on storage: a plant with 15 hours of storage needs a much larger mirror field per kW of turbine than one without storage, but it runs many more hours. That is why IRENA's capacity factor rose from 30% to 41% while costs fell.

Price vs fossil fuels

More expensive, but dispatchable

CSP costs slightly more per kWh than new coal or gas plants on average. Its value is the storage: it keeps producing after sunset, which PV alone cannot.

Earth heat · electricity and heat

Geothermal

Heat stored beneath the surface of the Earth, used to generate electricity where it is hot enough, to supply district heating networks, and, close to the surface, as the heat source for ground-source heat pumps. Unlike sun and wind, it is available all year round.

Electricity + heatBaseloadSite-dependent
916MWGeothermal power in Italy, almost all of the EU's capacityThinkGeoEnergy · 2025
17.2GWGeothermal power capacity worldwideThinkGeoEnergy · 2025
412Geothermal district heating systems operating in EuropeEGEC · 2024
88%Average capacity factor of new geothermal plantsIRENA · 2024
1 · Definition

What geothermal energy is

The EU Renewable Energy Directive defines geothermal energy as "energy stored in the form of heat beneath the surface of solid earth". The heat comes from the Earth's interior and from radioactive decay in the crust. Temperature rises with depth, on average by roughly 25–30 °C per kilometre in continental crust, and much faster in volcanic or tectonically active zones.

The resource is classified by temperature (enthalpy). High-temperature steam or water can drive turbines directly; moderate temperatures can still generate power with binary cycles, or supply heat directly. The shallow ground (tens to a few hundred metres), at a nearly constant 10–20 °C, serves as a heat source or sink for heat pumps.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Three scales of use

Power plants

Wells bring hot fluid to the surface to spin a turbine. 147 geothermal power plants were operating in Europe (including Türkiye and Iceland) at the end of 2024.

District heating

Hot water from aquifers 1–3 km deep heats whole neighbourhoods through a heat exchanger. Europe had 412 such systems at the end of 2024, with about 500 more in development.

Shallow geothermal

Ground-source heat pumps exchange heat with the ground through boreholes or buried pipes, for heating and cooling buildings. Their sales dropped in 2024 in every European country except Switzerland.

3 · Evolution

Born in Italy, stalled in the EU

Electricity from geothermal steam was first produced at Larderello, Tuscany, in 1904. Italy is still the only large EU producer and its capacity did not change in 2025. Spain has no geothermal power plant yet.

Spain: first steps

Power and heat
  1. 2023

    The Ministry for the Ecological Transition (MITECO) launches €120 million in aid for feasibility studies of deep geothermal energy.

  2. 2024

    One new geothermal district heating system opens in Spain (EGEC).

  3. 2025

    Gran Canaria enters its decisive exploration phase. Wells of up to 2.7 km were planned for the first half of 2026. Involcan says Gran Canaria could become the first Spanish island to generate baseload geothermal electricity.

Map

Where it is

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 1904

    At Larderello (Italy), geothermal steam drives a dynamo that lights five bulbs.

  2. 1913

    The first commercial geothermal power plant, 250 kW, opens at Larderello.

  3. 1958

    Wairakei (New Zealand) is the first plant to use a liquid-dominated (hot water) resource.

  4. 2025

    Eavor's closed-loop plant at Geretsried (Germany) delivers its first electricity to the grid.

Sources: Geothermal power; Eavor (see Sources).

4 · Types

Power cycles and heat systems

All geothermal systems move heat from rock to the surface with a fluid. They differ in fluid temperature and state, and in whether the reservoir is natural or engineered.

rare resource

Dry steam

The reservoir produces steam directly, which goes straight to the turbine. Larderello is the classic example.

most common

Flash

Pressurised hot water partly "flashes" to steam when the pressure drops. The steam drives the turbine and the brine is reinjected.

lower temperatures

Binary (ORC)

The geothermal fluid heats a second fluid with a low boiling point (Organic Rankine Cycle), which drives the turbine. It suits moderate temperatures, like most European resources outside Italy and Iceland.

pilot

Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS)

Hot but impermeable rock is stimulated to create flow paths between wells. This could unlock geothermal far from volcanic areas.

first grid power 2025

Closed loop

Fluid circulates inside sealed wells and never touches the reservoir. Eavor's plant at Geretsried (Bavaria) delivered its first electricity to the grid on 4 December 2025: four loops for 64 MWth and 8 MWe of combined heat and power.

Direct use and district heating

Hot water from a production well passes through a heat exchanger and is reinjected through a second well (a "doublet"). Used for networks, greenhouses and spas.

Ground-source heat pumps

Vertical boreholes or horizontal collectors exchange heat with the shallow ground. Because ground temperature is stable, EU default seasonal efficiency is 3.5, against 2.5–2.7 for air-source units.

5 · State of the art

A sector preparing to grow

More exploration

More than 17 exploration surveys were carried out in Europe in 2024, against 10 in 2023, and at least 10 3D seismic campaigns started in the first half of 2025 (EGEC).

New concepts reach the grid

Closed-loop systems (Geretsried) and EGS aim to make geothermal possible where there is no natural reservoir.

Slow global growth

Worldwide capacity grew by only 223 MW in 2025, to 17,173 MW. Italy, the US, Kenya and Japan added nothing.

6 · Economics

Expensive to drill, cheap to run

Most of the cost is upfront: exploration and drilling, with the risk that a well does not deliver enough flow or temperature. Once running, there is no fuel to buy and plants run most of the year, which keeps the LCOE moderate.

Ambient air · heat and cooling

Aerothermal

Heat pumps that take heat from the outdoor air, even in winter, and deliver it to a building at a higher temperature. For every kWh of electricity they use, they deliver several kWh of heat. The part taken from the air counts as renewable energy.

Heat + coolingRuns on electricityBuildings and industry
2.88MHeat pumps sold in 21 European countries, +13% on 2024EHPA · 2025
29.3MHeat pumps installed in those countriesEHPA · 2025
2.5Minimum seasonal performance (SPF) for a heat pump to count as renewable in the EUDecision 2013/114/EU
26.7%Renewable share of EU heating and cooling, up from 11.7% in 2004Eurostat · 2024
1 · Definition

What aerothermal energy is

The 2009 Renewable Energy Directive defined aerothermal energy as energy stored in the form of heat in the ambient air. The 2018 Directive groups it under "ambient energy". It is captured with a heat pump: a vapour-compression cycle in which a refrigerant evaporates in the outdoor unit (absorbing heat from the air), is compressed, and condenses in the indoor unit, releasing heat at a useful temperature.

Performance is measured by the coefficient of performance, COP = heat delivered ÷ electricity used, and over a whole season by the SCOP or SPF. The smaller the lift between outdoor and supply temperature, the higher the COP. The theoretical (Carnot) limit is Thot ÷ (Thot − Tcold), in kelvin.

How much of the heat is renewable

EU accounting rule (Commission Decision 2013/114/EU)
ERES = Qusable × (1 − 1/SPF)  ·  counts only if SPF > 1.15 × 1/η, with η = 45.5% → SPFmin = 2.5 for electric heat pumps

Example: a heat pump with SPF 3 delivering 10,000 kWh of heat uses about 3,333 kWh of electricity; the remaining 6,667 kWh counts as renewable ambient energy.

Animated demonstration

2 · Uses

Where air-source heat pumps work

Space heating

Air-to-water units feed radiators or underfloor heating. Low-temperature emitters raise efficiency.

Domestic hot water

Heat-pump water heaters and combined units. Since 2019 the Spanish building code (CTE HE4) accepts them to meet the renewable share of hot water in new buildings.

Cooling

Reversible units run the cycle backwards in summer. In Spain, reversible air-to-air units (split air conditioners) are the most common heat pumps.

Industry and networks

Large heat pumps supply low-temperature process heat and district heating. The IEA finds them cheaper over their lifetime than gas boilers in 17 EU countries for industrial heat.

3 · Evolution

A boom, a slump and a recovery

Sales peaked in 2022, during the gas price crisis, fell sharply in 2024 and recovered in 2025. France and Italy are the largest markets. In Germany sales grew 50% in 2025, and heat pumps reached half of the national space-heating market for the first time.

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 1852

    Lord Kelvin describes the heat pump principle.

  2. 1857

    Peter von Rittinger builds the first working heat pump, to evaporate brine in an Austrian salt works.

  3. 2009

    The Renewable Energy Directive (RED I) counts aerothermal heat captured by heat pumps as renewable energy.

  4. 2013

    Commission Decision 2013/114/EU sets how to count it; only heat pumps with SCOP above about 2.5 qualify.

  5. 2022

    Record European sales: 3.31 million heat pumps.

Sources: Heat pump (history); Decision 2013/114/EU; EHPA (see Sources).

4 · Types

Air-source heat pump families

All use the same refrigeration cycle and the outdoor air as source. They differ in what they heat (air or water), how they are split between indoor and outdoor units, and which refrigerant they use.

most sold in Europe

Air-to-air

Split or multi-split units that heat and cool room air directly. Cheapest, but no hot water.

central heating

Air-to-water

Monobloc (whole circuit outdoors) or split. Replaces a boiler in a wet heating system and can make hot water.

Hybrid

A heat pump paired with a gas boiler that takes over on the coldest days or at high temperatures.

Exhaust-air and water heaters

Recover heat from ventilation air, or heat a hot-water tank with a small built-in heat pump.

5 · State of the art

What is changing

Natural refrigerants

The 2024 F-gas Regulation (EU 2024/573) speeds up the move away from high-warming refrigerants to propane (R290) and CO₂ (R744).

Variable-speed compressors

Inverter-driven compressors follow the heat demand instead of switching on and off, which improves seasonal efficiency.

Running costs now favour heat pumps

The IEA finds heat pumps cheaper to run than gas boilers in almost all EU countries at 2025 prices, saving up to €800 a year. Higher upfront cost is still the main barrier.

6 · Economics

Running cost against a gas boiler

A heat pump's running cost is the electricity price divided by its seasonal efficiency. A boiler's is the gas price divided by its efficiency. Try your own numbers below. The default values are illustrative examples, not current market prices.

On upfront cost, the IEA (2026) states only that gas boilers remain significantly cheaper to buy and install. It finds lifetime ownership cost-competitive in 16 EU countries for homes (about one-third of residential space-heating demand). This guide has not found a recent, free, EU-wide CAPEX dataset for residential heat pumps.

Price vs fossil fuels

Heat pump against gas boiler

A heat pump is cheaper to run than a gas boiler whenever the electricity price is below SCOP × gas price ÷ boiler efficiency. With the example inputs of the calculator above (€0.20/kWh electricity, €0.08/kWh gas, SCOP 2.7, 92% boiler), each kWh of heat costs €0.074 against €0.087.

Water heat · heat and cooling

Hydrothermal

The word has two meanings in energy. In EU renewable-energy law and in Spanish practice (IDAE), hydrothermal energy is heat stored in surface water, such as rivers, lakes or the sea, recovered with water-source heat pumps. In geology, a hydrothermal system is a natural underground reservoir of hot water or steam, the resource behind most geothermal plants. This section covers both and how they differ.

Surface-water hydrothermal is the least used of the twelve technologies in this guide. It needs a river, lake, sea or aquifer close to the buildings it serves, and official statistics usually count it together with other heat-pump energy (Eurostat's "ambient heat"). That is why this section has fewer figures and charts than the others.

HeatHeat pumps on waterGeothermal reservoirs
70MWEsbjerg's seawater heat pump, the world's largest using CO₂ as refrigerant2024–25
≈25,000Households heated by the Esbjerg plantMAN Energy Solutions
+9%Growth in Spanish sales of water-to-water heat pumpsAFEC · 2025
1 · Definition

Two meanings of one word

EU law, IDAE

Surface-water heat

Directive 2009/28/EC defined hydrothermal energy as "energy stored in the form of heat in surface water". Directive 2018/2001 now includes it in "ambient energy", which covers heat in ambient air (except exhaust air) and in surface or sewage water. The heat is recovered with a water-source heat pump.

geology

Hydrothermal reservoirs

Permeable rock holding hot water or steam that can flow to a well. These are the conventional geothermal resources, liquid-dominated or vapour-dominated, as opposed to hot dry rock that must be stimulated (EGS). See the Geothermal section for power plants.

What they share: both use water as the carrier of low- or high-grade heat. Where they differ: surface water is close to ambient temperature and needs a heat pump. A geothermal reservoir is hot enough to use directly or to generate electricity.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Applications

District heating from the sea or rivers

Large heat pumps lift seawater or river heat to 60–90 °C for city networks, as in Esbjerg (Denmark).

Buildings near water

Water-to-water heat pumps in hotels, ports and waterfront buildings use a stable source temperature, which gives better winter efficiency than air.

Cooling

Sea, lake or river water absorbs heat rejected by chillers, or cools buildings directly when it is cold enough.

Geothermal aquifers

Hydrothermal reservoirs feed geothermal district heating. The Paris Basin (Dogger aquifer) and the Bavarian Molasse Basin around Munich are Europe's best-known examples.

3 · Evolution

A small but growing niche

No official EU or Spanish statistic separates surface-water heat from other ambient heat: Eurostat reports it together with aerothermal energy as heat pump output, and IDAE groups aerothermal and hydrothermal energy together. The available indicators are equipment sales and individual large projects.

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 1938

    Zurich's city hall is heated by a heat pump using water from the Limmat river, one of the first large heat pumps.

  2. 2009

    RED I recognises hydrothermal energy (heat from surface water) as renewable.

  3. 2024

    Esbjerg (Denmark): the world's largest seawater heat pump using CO₂ as refrigerant supplies the city's district heating.

Sources: Heat pump (history); Esbjerg project (see Sources).

4 · Types

System types

SystemHeat sourceHow it worksTypical output

5 · State of the art

Esbjerg: a seawater heat pump at city scale

Capacity

70 MW of heat from two identical CO₂ heat pumps working in parallel, in a single-stage transcritical cycle.

Source

14,000 m³/h of North Sea water, taken about 600 m offshore and returned about 1.5 km offshore.

Output

Supply at 60–90 °C, return around 35 °C, for the Esbjerg and Varde networks (about 25,000 households). The first unit was commissioned in late 2024.

Sources: IEA HPT Annex 57 case study; pv magazine (Nov 2024).

6 · Economics

Costs

The economics follow the same logic as other heat pumps: running cost ≈ electricity price ÷ seasonal efficiency. A water source at a steady temperature gives a higher efficiency in winter than air. That saving is offset by the cost of intakes, filters and heat exchangers that resist fouling and corrosion, plus water-use permits.

This guide has not found published, free CAPEX or LCOH figures for European surface-water heat pump projects, including Esbjerg, so it does not quote any. Use the running-cost calculator in the Aerothermal section with a higher SPF to compare.

Price vs fossil fuels

Heat pump against gas boiler

The same rule as for air-source heat pumps applies: a water-source heat pump is cheaper to run when electricity costs less than SCOP × gas price ÷ boiler efficiency. Water is warmer than winter air and its temperature is stable, so water-source units usually reach a higher SCOP, which widens the margin. No free, published cost figures for European surface-water projects were found, so no chart is shown.

7 · Operation

Operating hours

Statistics of hours or energy delivered by surface-water heat pumps are not published separately in the EU or Spain. Large district heating heat pumps such as Esbjerg are designed to run as base load through the heating season. For geothermal hydrothermal reservoirs, see Geothermal, Operation.

Thermal plants · electricity and heat

Biomass

Energy from organic matter: wood and forest residues, agricultural waste, energy crops and the organic part of municipal waste. It can be burned, gasified or digested into biogas, and it is the only renewable fuel that can be stored and burned on demand like coal or gas.

Electricity + heatDispatchableFuel supply chain
54%Bioenergy share of all renewable energy used in the EUBioenergy Europe
156TWhEU electricity from bioenergy, 5.6% of the mixEmber · 2025
6.4TWhSpanish electricity from bioenergy, 2.2% of the mixEmber · 2025
22bcmBiogas and biomethane produced in EuropeEBA · 2024
1 · Definition

What biomass energy is

Biomass is the biodegradable fraction of products, waste and residues from agriculture, forestry and related industries, and the biodegradable part of industrial and municipal waste. Plants capture CO₂ as they grow, and burning them releases it again. That is why EU rules count biomass as renewable, provided it meets the sustainability and emission-saving criteria of the Renewable Energy Directive.

Unlike solar and wind, biomass is a fuel. A biomass power plant works like a coal plant (a boiler raising steam for a Rankine cycle), and its output can be scheduled. The trade-off is a fuel supply chain: collection, transport, drying and storage.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Mostly heat, some electricity

Heating in homes

Stoves and boilers burning firewood, chips or pellets. Biomass covers around 22% of residential heat in the EU.

District heating

Biomass is the largest input to EU district heating networks, at around 32% of the mix.

Electricity and CHP

Dedicated power plants and combined heat and power (CHP) plants, often at sawmills, pulp mills and agri-food factories that have their own residues.

Biogas and biomethane

Anaerobic digestion of manure, food waste or sludge produces biogas for engines and CHP, or, once upgraded, biomethane for the gas grid.

3 · Evolution

Rapid growth, then a plateau

EU bioelectricity grew more than fivefold between 2000 and 2021, then levelled off and eased slightly. Spain's output is small, about 2% of its mix, and has roughly quadrupled since 2000.

Map

Where it is

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 2018

    RED II sets sustainability and greenhouse-gas criteria for solid biomass and biogas used for power and heat.

  2. 2021

    EU electricity from bioenergy peaks at 171.6 TWh.

  3. 2024

    Europe counts 1,620 biomethane plants, 111 more than a year before.

Sources: Directive (EU) 2018/2001; Ember; EBA (see Sources).

4 · Types

Feedstocks and conversion routes

All routes release the energy that plants stored by photosynthesis. They differ in the feedstock (dry or wet), the process (thermal or biological) and the final energy carrier.

most common

Direct combustion

Grate or fluidised-bed boilers burn chips, pellets, straw or residues to raise steam (power, CHP) or hot water (heating).

Co-firing and conversion

Biomass burned alongside coal, or a coal plant converted to burn only biomass.

Gasification

Partial oxidation at high temperature turns biomass into a combustible syngas (CO + H₂) for engines, turbines or fuel synthesis.

Waste-to-energy

Incineration of municipal waste with energy recovery. Only the biodegradable fraction counts as renewable.

growing

Anaerobic digestion

Bacteria break down wet organic matter (manure, food waste, sewage sludge) without oxygen into biogas, mainly methane and CO₂.

Biomethane upgrading

Removing CO₂ and impurities produces biomethane that can be injected into the gas grid. Europe had 1,620 biomethane plants at the end of 2024, 111 more than a year earlier.

RouteFeedstockProductFinal use
CombustionDry: wood, chips, pellets, strawHeat / steamHeating, power, CHP
GasificationDry biomassSyngasPower, CHP, fuels
Anaerobic digestionWet: manure, food waste, sludgeBiogas → biomethaneCHP, gas grid, transport
Waste-to-energyMunicipal wasteHeat / steamPower, district heating
5 · State of the art

Negative emissions and biomethane

BECCS

Capturing the CO₂ from biomass combustion and storing it underground removes CO₂ from the atmosphere. Stockholm Exergi's plant at Värtaverket is designed to capture up to 800,000 t of CO₂ a year from 2028, shipped to the Northern Lights store under the North Sea.

Biomethane scale-up

Europe produced 5.2 bcm of biomethane in 2024 (4.3 bcm in the EU-27), and 25 countries now produce it.

Sustainability limits

Biomass supply is finite, and its climate benefit depends on where it comes from and how fast forests regrow. EU sustainability criteria and residue-first strategies respond to this.

6 · Economics

A fuel cost that sun and wind do not have

Fuel can be the largest share of a biomass plant's operating costs, so its LCOE depends on local feedstock prices and transport distances.

Price vs fossil fuels

About the same as gas

Bioenergy power costs about the same as a new gas plant and more than coal on average, because, like them, it has to buy fuel.

Thermal plants · electricity

Nuclear

Fission of uranium nuclei releases heat that raises steam for a turbine. Nuclear is the largest single source of electricity in the EU and, by Red Eléctrica's count, the second-largest in Spain in 2025. The EU is extending the life of existing reactors while Spain follows a phase-out calendar.

ElectricityBaseloadVery low CO₂
652TWhEU nuclear generation, 23.3% of the mixEmber · 2025
101Reactors in 12 EU countriesEuropean Commission · end 2024
7reactorsIn Spain: 7,117 MW, 19.0% of generationREE / Foro Nuclear · 2025
7,284hEquivalent full-power hours of the Spanish fleetForo Nuclear · 2025
1 · Definition

What nuclear power is

When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it splits into two lighter nuclei and releases about 200 MeV of energy plus two or three new neutrons, which sustain a chain reaction. A moderator (usually water) slows the neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission, control rods absorb neutrons to regulate power, and a coolant carries the heat out of the core.

The heat then drives a conventional steam cycle. Because steam conditions are limited by the reactor materials, light-water reactors convert roughly a third of the heat into electricity.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Steady output, long lives

Baseload electricity

Reactors usually run near full power, because almost all their cost is fixed. Some fleets, such as France's, also vary output to follow demand.

Long-term operation

Many European reactors were designed for 40 years and are being licensed to run for 50, 60 years or more. Slovenia's Krško has been extended to 2043.

Heat and other uses

A few plants supply district heat or process heat. Small modular reactors are being studied for heat, hydrogen and industrial sites.

3 · Evolution

Peak in 2004, phase-outs and life extensions

EU nuclear output peaked in 2004, then fell with closures in Germany, Belgium and elsewhere, and dropped sharply in 2022 because of corrosion inspections in France. Spain's fleet has produced a steady 52–64 TWh a year.

Spain: timeline

From the first reactor to the phase-out plan
  1. 1968

    José Cabrera (Zorita), Spain's first nuclear plant, connects to the grid.

  2. 1984

    A nuclear moratorium halts plants under construction, such as Lemóniz and Valdecaballeros.

  3. 2006

    Zorita closes. Santa María de Garoña stops in 2012 and closes for good in 2017.

  4. 2019

    Owners and Enresa agree a closure calendar: all seven reactors shut between 2027 and 2035.

  5. 2024

    The Enresa waste-management fee rises 30%, from €7.98 to €10.36 per MWh.

  6. 2026

    The nuclear regulator (CSN) backs extending Almaraz. The government extends its operation to 8 June 2030, instead of 2027 and 2028.

4 · Types

Reactor designs in the EU

All commercial reactors in the EU are thermal-neutron reactors that drive a steam turbine. They differ in moderator, coolant and fuel enrichment, and in whether the steam is raised inside the core or in separate steam generators.

most common

PWR (pressurised water)

Water kept liquid at high pressure cools the core and transfers heat through steam generators to a separate steam loop. Six of Spain's seven reactors and all of France's are PWRs. Russian-designed VVERs in Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, Bulgaria and Finland are also PWRs.

single loop

BWR (boiling water)

Water boils inside the core and the steam goes straight to the turbine. Simpler, with no steam generators, but the turbine hall is part of the radioactive circuit. Examples: Cofrentes (Spain), Olkiluoto 1–2 (Finland), several Swedish units.

Romania

PHWR / CANDU

Heavy water as moderator allows natural (unenriched) uranium, and fuel is changed while running. Cernavodă's two units are the EU's only examples; two more are planned by 2031.

Generation III+

EPR

A large evolutionary PWR (about 1,600–1,670 MW) with added passive and redundant safety systems. Olkiluoto 3 (Finland) started regular operation in April 2023; Flamanville 3 (France) reached full power in December 2025.

development

SMRs and Generation IV

Small modular reactors (typically up to about 300 MW) aim to cut cost and build time through factory production. The European Commission cites estimates of 17–53 GW of SMRs in the EU by 2050.

5 · State of the art

Big projects, big overruns

Flamanville 3

Construction started in 2007 and was planned to take 54 months. The cost estimate rose from €3.3 billion to €13.2 billion (EDF, 2022); the French Court of Auditors puts it at €23.7 billion including financing costs. 1,669 MW gross; full power in December 2025.

Olkiluoto 3

1,600 MW. Construction began in 2005 and regular production in April 2023, about 14 years late and at roughly three times the initial budget.

EU outlook

The Commission expects about 98 GW in 2025 and 109 GW in 2050 in its base case. It estimates €241 billion of investment by 2050: €205 billion for new build and €36 billion for life extensions.

Spanish taxes and fees

Specific to nuclear

Since 1 July 2024 Spanish reactors pay €10.36/MWh to Enresa, the public company that manages radioactive waste and decommissioning (previously €7.98/MWh). Foro Nuclear estimates the fee at about €580 million a year.

Price vs fossil fuels

The most expensive new plants, in the US

In Lazard's US analysis, new nuclear has the highest cost per MWh of all options, mainly because of construction cost and time. Existing plants, already paid off, are much cheaper to run, and LCOE does not value nuclear's steady output or its 60–80 year life.

Thermal plants · electricity and heat

Coal

Hard coal and lignite burned in steam power plants. Coal was Europe's backbone fuel for a century and still produced 30% of EU electricity in 2000. It has collapsed since 2018 under carbon pricing and cheaper renewables, and Spain has almost stopped using it.

Electricity + heatDispatchableHighest CO₂ per kWh
258TWhEU coal generation, 9.2% of the mix (800 TWh in 2000)Ember · 2025
0.3%Coal share of Spanish generation (36% in 2000)Ember · 2025
970g/kWhLifecycle CO₂e intensity of EU coal power, against 211 for the average kWhEmber · 2025
€74/t CO₂Average EU carbon allowance priceESMA · 2025
1 · Definition

What a coal power plant is

Coal is a fossil fuel formed from plant matter buried and compressed over millions of years. The longer and deeper the burial, the higher its carbon content and heating value: lignite (brown coal) is wet and low-grade, while sub-bituminous, bituminous and anthracite (hard coal) are progressively richer.

In a pulverised-coal plant, coal is ground to powder and burned in a boiler that raises high-pressure steam. The steam drives a turbine in a Rankine cycle and is condensed and pumped back. Higher steam pressure and temperature mean higher efficiency and less CO₂ per kWh.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Power, heat and reserve

Electricity

Large power stations next to mines (lignite) or ports (imported hard coal). Germany and Poland produced more than 74% of the EU's coal power in 2025.

Combined heat and power

In Central and Eastern Europe many coal plants also supply district heating, which slows their closure.

Reserve

Some plants are kept only for emergencies. Spain's Alcúdia plant (Mallorca) is capped at 500 hours a year until a second link to the mainland is built.

3 · Evolution

From backbone to residual

Spain: timeline

The end of coal power
  1. 2018

    Subsidised coal mining ends at the close of the year.

  2. 2020

    Seven coal plants close on 30 June, unable to meet EU emission standards.

  3. 2024

    As Pontes (Galicia, 1.4 GW), the largest, stops for good.

  4. 2025

    Aboño II (Asturias) is converted to gas in July. Spain's power system runs 74 days in a row without coal (3 July to 16 September).

  5. Now

    Aboño I runs a limited number of hours; owners have asked to close Soto 3 and Los Barrios; Alcúdia is emergency backup. The national commitment is to be coal-free by 2030.

Sources: Beyond Fossil Fuels (Nov 2025); REE; Maldita (2020).

  2. 1957

4 · Types

Fuels and plant technologies

Every coal plant burns carbon to raise steam. What changes is the fuel quality, which sets the CO₂ per kWh, and the steam conditions, which set the efficiency.

Steam conditions and efficiency

Pulverised-coal plants

Fluidised bed (CFB)

Coal burns in a bed of hot sand kept in suspension by air. It accepts low-grade fuels and can co-fire biomass; limestone in the bed captures sulphur.

IGCC

Coal is gasified and the syngas burned in a combined cycle. Spain had one of Europe's few plants, ELCOGAS in Puertollano (335 MW), now closed.

Carbon capture (CCS)

Capturing CO₂ from flue gas costs energy and money. No commercial coal plant in the EU operates with CCS.

5 · State of the art

The end game in Europe

Overtaken by every other source

EU coal was overtaken by nuclear in 1994, by gas in 2019, by hydro and wind in 2023, and by solar in 2024 (Eurostat via ANSA).

Two countries left

Germany (104 TWh) and Poland (87 TWh) both hit record lows in 2025. Coal still supplies about half of Poland's electricity.

Carbon price

At €74/t, a subcritical plant emitting 0.83 t/MWh pays about €61 per MWh in CO₂ alone, before fuel and O&M.

Wind · electricity

Wind power

Turbines that turn the kinetic energy of moving air into rotation and then into electricity. Wind is the EU's second-largest source of electricity and, by Red Eléctrica's count, Spain's largest for the third year running.

ElectricityVariable outputOnshore and offshore
480TWhEU wind generation, 17.1% of the mixEmber · 2025
21.6%Wind share of Spanish generation, 58,801 GWhREE · 2025
33.2GWWind capacity in Spain, second in Europe after GermanyWindEurope · 2025
0.034$/kWhGlobal average LCOE of new onshore wind, the cheapest new sourceIRENA · 2024
1 · Definition

What wind power is

The power carried by wind through a rotor of area A is P = ½·ρ·A·v³. Because it grows with the cube of wind speed, doubling the speed gives eight times the power, so siting is critical. No rotor can capture more than 16/27 (59.3%) of that power, the Betz limit; modern turbines reach a power coefficient of about 0.45–0.50.

A typical turbine starts producing at about 3 m/s, reaches rated power at 11–13 m/s and stops at about 25 m/s to protect itself. Between rated and cut-out speed the blades pitch (rotate on their own axis) to keep power constant.

Worked example: a 236 m rotor sweeps 43,742 m². At 10 m/s and ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ the wind carries about 26.8 MW through it; the Betz limit caps capture at about 15.9 MW.

How it works

Animated demonstration

A step-by-step animation of the process. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

2 · Uses

Onshore, offshore and repowering

Onshore farms

The EU had 224.5 GW onshore at the end of 2025, covering 16% of demand. Spain's largest farm, Gecama (Cuenca, 329 MW), has approval to add 250 MW of solar and a 100 MW / 200 MWh battery.

Offshore farms

21.5 GW in the EU, covering 3% of demand. Spain has only about 7 MW at sea: its deep coastal waters suit floating turbines, such as the 2 MW DemoSATH (Basque Country, 2023).

Repowering

Old farms on the best sites get fewer, larger turbines. A Spanish support scheme replaces 1,205 old turbines with 167 new ones, raising capacity factors from about 20% to about 35%.

Spain's offshore plan

The 2023 marine spatial plans (POEM) reserve about 5,000 km² in five areas. The consultation for the first auction opened in February 2026, with a target of 3 GW by 2030.

3 · Evolution

Spain led early, then paused

Spain went from 8.5 GW in 2004 to 22.8 GW in 2012. The 2012 moratorium (Royal Decree-law 1/2012) stopped growth: only 204 MW were added from 2012 to 2015. Auctions in 2016–2017 (about 4.1 GW of wind) restarted it.

Milestones

Key moments

  1. 1887

    James Blyth's turbine in Scotland is the first to produce electricity.

  2. 1888

    Charles Brush builds a 12 kW wind dynamo in Cleveland (US).

  3. 1891

    Poul la Cour starts wind power research at Askov (Denmark).

  4. 1956

    The 200 kW Gedser turbine (Denmark) sets the three-blade design used today.

  5. 1991

    Vindeby (Denmark), the world's first offshore wind farm.

  6. 2012

    Spain reaches 22.8 GW; the moratorium then halts growth for four years.

  7. 2025

    A 26 MW turbine with a 310 m rotor (Dongfang, China).

Sources: History of wind power; WindEurope, offshoreWIND.biz (see Sources).

4 · Types

Rotors, foundations and drivetrains

All wind turbines convert the momentum of the air into shaft torque. They differ in rotor axis, where they stand and how the slow rotor speed reaches the generator.

dominant

Horizontal axis (HAWT)

Three blades upwind of the tower, a yaw system that turns the nacelle into the wind. Highest efficiency.

niche

Vertical axis (Darrieus, Savonius)

Accepts wind from any direction and keeps the generator at ground level, but with lower efficiency and fatigue problems. Mainly small-scale.

shallow water

Fixed-bottom

Monopile (a single steel tube, the most common), jacket (steel lattice for deeper or harder seabeds) or gravity base. Used up to roughly 50–60 m depth.

deep water

Floating

Spar (deep ballasted cylinder), semi-submersible (buoyant columns, assembled in port) or tension-leg platform. Spain's demonstrators use concrete floating structures.

Geared

A gearbox raises the rotor speed (about 5–15 rpm) for a faster, lighter generator, often a doubly fed induction generator (DFIG). Cheaper, but the gearbox needs maintenance.

Direct drive

A large, slow permanent-magnet generator with no gearbox. Fewer moving parts, but heavier and dependent on rare-earth magnets.

5 · State of the art

Bigger rotors, further from shore

Record turbines

Dongfang's 26 MW turbine (China, 2025) has a 310 m rotor. Europe's largest in commercial use is the Vestas V236 (15 MW, 236 m rotor), installed at Germany's 960 MW He Dreiht farm.

Average size keeps rising

Turbines installed in Europe in 2025 averaged 5.2 MW onshore and 10.7 MW offshore. Orders placed in 2025 averaged 6.1 MW and 14.6 MW.

Blade recycling

85–90% of a turbine's mass is already recyclable; the composite blades are the problem. Recyclable resins and landfill bans in several countries are the response.

Thermal plants · electricity and heat

Natural gas

Gas turbines burn natural gas and drive a generator directly; combined-cycle plants recover the hot exhaust to raise steam for a second turbine. Gas is the most flexible large source in the system, and the one that most often sets the electricity price.

Electricity + heatDispatchable, fastBrayton + Rankine
467TWhEU gas generation, 16.7% of the mix, up 8% on 2024Ember · 2025
26.3GWCombined-cycle capacity in Spain; output rose 27.9% in 2025REE · 2025
64.18%Record combined-cycle efficiency (gross), Keadby 2, UKGuinness · 2024
≈1,740hEquivalent hours of Spanish combined cycles, against ≈2,540 in 2010REE-derived · 2025
1 · Definition

What a gas power plant is

A gas turbine works on the Brayton cycle: a compressor pressurises air, fuel burns in the combustor at constant pressure, and the hot gas expands through the turbine, which drives both the compressor and the generator. Turbine inlet temperatures are so high that the blades are cooled with compressor air and protected by ceramic coatings.

Alone, a gas turbine converts about 20–35% of the fuel energy into electricity (the best large frames reach 43%). Its exhaust leaves at around 600 °C. In a combined cycle, a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) uses that exhaust to raise steam for a Rankine cycle, so overall efficiency reaches about 60%: ηCC = ηGT + (1 − ηGT)·ηST.

Example: ηGT = 0.42 and ηST = 0.35 give 0.42 + 0.58 × 0.35 ≈ 0.62.

How it works

2 · Uses

Backup, flexibility and industry

Flexible backup

Open-cycle turbines start in 5–11 minutes; combined cycles in 30–90 minutes from hot and 2–4 hours from cold. They fill the gaps left by sun, wind and water.

Voltage control and security

Their synchronous generators control voltage and add inertia. After the 2025 blackout REE scheduled 39% more combined-cycle output for security from May to December than a year earlier.

Industrial cogeneration

CHP plants in food, chemicals, paper and ceramics produce heat and power together. In Spain cogeneration fell from about 12% to about 6% of generation in five years (ACOGEN).

Islands

In the Canary Islands combined cycles made 41.3% of 2025 electricity, but burn gasoil because there is no natural gas supply. In the Balearics they made 62.3%.

3 · Evolution

Spain's "dash for gas" and its aftermath

Spain had four combined-cycle plants (2.8 GW) in 2002 and 27 GW in 2010. As renewables grew and demand fell, output collapsed: in 2014 the fleet ran only about 950 equivalent hours. Gas rose again in 2022 when drought cut hydro, and in 2025 after the blackout.

5 · State of the art

Efficiency, hydrogen and carbon capture

H-class turbines

Keadby 2 (UK, Siemens Energy HL) holds the record at 64.18% corrected gross efficiency (2024). EDF's Bouchain (France) set a 62.22% net record in 2016. No certified net figure above 63% was found.

Hydrogen blending

Large turbines from GE and Siemens Energy accept up to 50% hydrogen by volume; manufacturers target 100% capability by 2030.

Carbon capture

Net Zero Teesside (UK, 742 MW) took its final investment decision in December 2024, to capture up to 2 Mt of CO₂ a year from 2028. Capture raises capital cost sharply and uses about 16% more fuel per kWh (EIA data).

Price vs fossil fuels

Compared with coal and renewables

Gas is itself a fossil fuel. Its new-plant LCOE is above coal's (global average, without carbon costs) and about twice that of new solar or onshore wind. In 2025 its short-run cost in Spain was about €86/MWh, two thirds of it fuel (see Economics).

Water · electricity and storage

Hydropower and pumped storage

Water falling from a height spins a turbine. Reservoir plants can store water and choose when to generate, and pumped-storage plants pump water uphill when electricity is cheap and generate when it is expensive, which makes them Europe's largest electricity store.

ElectricityDispatchableStorage
325TWhEU hydro generation, 11.6% of the mix, 12% less than in 2024Ember · 2025
17.1GWHydro capacity in Spain; 33,685 GWh in 2025REE · 2025
3.3GWPumped-storage capacity in SpainREE · 2025
>90%Share of EU energy storage provided by pumped hydroJRC
1 · Definition

What hydropower is

A hydro plant converts the potential energy of water into electricity: P = η·ρ·g·Q·H, where Q is the flow (m³/s), H the head (height difference, m) and η the combined efficiency of penstock, turbine and generator. With no thermal cycle, the overall conversion can exceed 90%.

Example: Q = 100 m³/s, H = 100 m and η = 0.90 give P = 1,000 × 9.81 × 100 × 100 × 0.90 ≈ 88 MW.

How it works

2 · Uses

Energy, storage and grid services

Run-of-river

Little or no storage: output follows the river flow.

Reservoir plants

A dam stores water so generation can be shifted to when it is most needed, from hours to seasons.

Pumped storage

Two reservoirs at different heights. The plant stores energy rather than producing it: it pumps with surplus electricity and generates at peak, with about 80% round-trip efficiency (NREL). Compared with other stores on the Energy storage page.

Grid services and black start

Hydro units ramp in seconds, provide inertia and can start without external power. On 28 April 2025 Spanish hydro plants with black-start capability helped restart the Iberian grid (ENTSO-E).

3 · Evolution

A mature fleet that follows the rain

Most large dams were built before 1990, so capacity barely changes, but output swings with rainfall. Spain's hydro output fell about 40% in the 2022 drought, the lowest on record, then rose 41% in 2023 and 35.5% in 2024 (REE).
