4 · Types

Turbines and plant designs

All hydro turbines turn the energy of moving water into shaft torque. Impulse turbines use free jets at atmospheric pressure; reaction turbines run fully submerged. The head and flow decide which is best.

TurbinePrincipleTypical headNotes
PeltonImpulse (jets on buckets)50–1,300 mHigh head, low flow
FrancisReaction, fixed blades25–350 mThe most widely used; reversible versions pump
KaplanReaction, adjustable blades2–40 mLow head, high flow, wide operating range

Head ranges from the small-hydro guide of Penche (2004), as tabulated by Sustainable Energy Research; other sources quote wider ranges. Size classes (IRENA): large ≥100 MW, small 1–20 MW (EU "small hydro" ≤20 MW).

Open vs closed loop

Open-loop pumped storage is connected to a river; closed-loop uses two reservoirs isolated from natural watercourses.

Fixed vs variable speed

A fixed-speed pump runs at full power or not at all. Variable-speed units, with a frequency converter, can regulate power while pumping and respond faster.

5 · State of the art

Storage for a renewable system

New pumped storage

Europe has a 52.9 GW pumped-storage pipeline, 3 GW of it under construction (IHA). Spain's IDAE calls have funded projects of over 2 GW, with a second call raised to €165 million in 2026.

Variable speed

Portugal's Frades II (780 MW) uses variable-speed units that stay stable four times longer during grid disturbances than fixed-speed ones (IRENA).

Environmental limits

Reservoirs lose about 0.7% of volume a year to sediment, and EU rivers have about 450,000 barriers. Spain's 2022–2027 basin plans set ecological flows for all water bodies.

Price vs fossil fuels

Cheaper than new fossil plants

New hydropower is cheaper than new coal or gas on average, although costs depend heavily on the site. Old dams, already paid off, are among the cheapest plants in the system.

Fundamentals · thermodynamics and electrical machines

How heat and motion become electricity

Most power plants share two steps. A thermodynamic cycle turns heat into the rotation of a turbine shaft, and a generator turns that rotation into alternating current for the grid. Hydro and wind skip the heat cycle, and photovoltaics skip both. This page explains the common principles behind the technology sections.

Power cyclesGeneratorGrid
1 · The limit

Why no heat engine reaches 100%

A heat engine takes heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work and rejects the rest to a cold sink: the condenser, a cooling tower, a river or the atmosphere. The second law of thermodynamics sets a ceiling, the Carnot efficiency: ηmax = 1 − Tcold/Thot, with temperatures in kelvin. Real cycles reach well below it, but the rule explains the whole industry's effort to raise turbine inlet temperatures and lower condenser temperatures.

2 · Power cycles

Rankine, Brayton and the reverse cycle

Temperature–entropy (T–s) diagrams show each cycle as a loop: heat enters along the top, leaves along the bottom, and the area enclosed is the net work. Choose a cycle.

4 · Combined cycle

Stacking two cycles

A gas turbine rejects its heat at about 600 °C, hot enough to run a steam cycle. The combined efficiency is ηCC = ηGT + (1 − ηGT) · ηST, where ηST is the share of the exhaust heat the steam cycle turns into work.

5 · From turbine to grid

Animated demonstration

The electrical half of a power plant, step by step. It plays automatically; pause it or jump to any step with the numbered buttons.

6 · The generator

Synchronous machines and 50 Hz

Almost every thermal and hydro plant uses a synchronous generator. Its rotor is an electromagnet fed with direct current (the excitation); as the shaft turns, its magnetic field sweeps the three sets of stator coils and induces a three-phase alternating voltage (Faraday's law). The frequency is tied to the shaft speed: n = 60·f / p, with n in rpm, f in hertz and p the number of pole pairs. Europe's grid runs at 50 Hz, so every synchronous generator connected to it turns in lockstep at a fixed speed.

Two control loops act on each machine. The governor adjusts steam, gas or water flow to control power (and, together with all the others, frequency). The automatic voltage regulator (AVR) adjusts the excitation current to control voltage and reactive power. A step-up transformer then raises the voltage to transmission level, 220 or 400 kV in Spain, so the same power travels with less current and lower losses (losses grow with the square of the current).

MachinePolesSpeed at 50 HzWhy
Gas and coal steam turbines23,000 rpmSmall, fast turbines are cheapest per MW
Large nuclear turbines41,500 rpmHuge low-pressure stages; slower speed keeps blade-tip stresses acceptable
Hydro (example)24250 rpmWater turbines are slow, so the generator has many poles
Wind (direct drive)–≈10 rpmConnected through a power converter, so the speed is not tied to 50 Hz

Speeds follow from n = 60·f/p with f = 50 Hz. The hydro row is an example: real hydro generators have from a few to over 100 poles depending on head and turbine.

7 · Inertia

The flywheel that keeps the grid steady

Every synchronous generator and turbine is a heavy rotating mass. When a large plant trips, the others slow down slightly and release their kinetic energy, which buys time for the governors and reserves to react. The inertia constant H (seconds) measures this stored energy relative to the machine's rating. For the system, the initial rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) after losing a share ΔP of generation is approximately RoCoF ≈ ΔP · f0 / (2·H).

Solar panels and most wind turbines connect through inverters and add no inertia by themselves. As they replace synchronous plants, system inertia falls and frequency moves faster. ENTSO-E recommends keeping system inertia of at least 2 MWs/MVA for more than half of the year by 2035; synchronous condensers, batteries and grid-forming inverters can supply it.

8 · Inverters

Grid-following and grid-forming

most PV and wind today

Grid-following

Measures the grid voltage with a phase-locked loop and injects current in step with it. It needs a stable voltage set by other machines, so it cannot run a grid alone.

emerging

Grid-forming

Creates its own voltage waveform, like a synchronous generator, and can respond almost instantly to disturbances. It can provide synthetic inertia and help restart a grid.

Wind generator types

Type 1: fixed-speed induction generator. Type 2: induction with variable rotor resistance. Type 3: doubly fed induction generator (DFIG), with a partial converter. Type 4: full converter, usually with a permanent-magnet generator; the most common in new large turbines.

See also the Overview sections on the 2025 blackout and on future challenges.

System · storage

Energy storage

Storage does not generate energy: it moves it in time, from when it is produced to when it is needed. As sun and wind take a larger share, storage becomes the partner that fills the gaps. There are two big families, electrical and thermal, and this page explains how they work, how they differ and what they have in common.

ElectricalThermalShifts energy in time
36GWhBatteries installed in Europe in 2025; the fleet passed 100 GWhSolarPower Europe · 2025
46GWPumped-storage hydro in the EU, the largest store by farCETO · 2023
22.5GWStorage target for Spain in 2030, against 3.4 GW at the end of 2025PNIEC · REE
70$/kWhAverage price of a stationary battery pack, 45% less than in 2024BNEF · 2025
1 · Definition

Power, energy and duration

A store is described by three numbers. Power (MW) is how fast it can charge or discharge. Energy (MWh) is how much it holds. Their ratio is the duration: a 50 MW battery with 200 MWh runs for 4 hours at full power. The fourth key number is the round-trip efficiency: the share of the energy put in that comes back out.

Storage earns its value from the difference between when energy is cheap or abundant (sunny middays, windy nights) and when it is scarce (evening peaks, still winter weeks). It also provides fast grid services: frequency control, voltage support and, increasingly, inertia.

Example: a battery with 85% round-trip efficiency that charges at €10/MWh must sell above about €12/MWh just to recover the energy lost (10 ÷ 0.85), before counting its investment.

2 · Two families

Electrical and thermal storage

Electrical storage takes electricity and gives electricity back, storing it in between as chemical, potential or other energy. Thermal storage stores heat (or cold) in a hot or cold material and gives it back as heat, which can be used directly or turned into electricity in a turbine.

Electrical storageThermal storage
Energy in → outElectricity → electricityHeat (or electricity) → heat, sometimes → electricity
Stored asChemical (batteries, hydrogen), gravitational (pumped hydro)Sensible heat (hot water, molten salt, rocks), latent heat (phase-change materials)
ExamplesLithium-ion batteries, pumped hydro, hydrogenCSP molten-salt tanks, hot-water tanks and pits for district heating, industrial heat stores
Round-trip efficiency≈85% Li-ion, ≈80% pumped hydro, ≈40% hydrogenHigh if heat is used as heat; much lower if heat is turned back into electricity (limited by the power cycle)
Cost per kWh storedHigher: battery packs ≈$70/kWhe (stationary)Lower: molten salt ≈$26–40/kWhth
Typical durationHours (batteries) to days (pumped hydro); seasons (hydrogen)Hours (CSP) to seasons (large water pits)
Main useBalancing the power grid, evening peaks, grid servicesHeating, industry, and dispatchable CSP power

What they share

Both shift energy in time and decouple production from demand. Both are described by power, energy, duration and efficiency, and both lose some energy while they wait: self-discharge in batteries, heat leaking through insulation in thermal stores. Both make variable renewables more useful.

Where they differ

Electricity is the most valuable and flexible form of energy, so storing it costs more. Heat is cheaper to store, but a kWh of heat is worth less: turning it back into electricity loses more than half of it (see the Fundamentals page). So thermal storage is best when the final need is heat, or when, as in CSP, the heat is already there before the turbine.

kWhe = kilowatt-hour of electricity; kWhth = kilowatt-hour of heat. Costs per kWhe and per kWhth are not directly comparable. Sources in the Economics section below.

3 · Types

The main storage technologies

electrical

Lithium-ion batteries

Electrochemical cells charged through an inverter. Respond in milliseconds, usually 2–4 hours of storage, about 85% round-trip efficiency and a 15-year life at about one cycle a day (NREL). They can work as grid-forming inverters.

electrical

Pumped-storage hydro

Pumps water uphill and turbines it later; about 80% round-trip efficiency, long life and many hours of storage. Over 90% of EU storage capacity. See Hydropower.

electrical

Hydrogen

Electrolysers turn electricity into hydrogen (70–80% efficient); it can be stored for months, for example in salt caverns, and turned back into power in fuel cells or turbines. Round trip about 40% (Sandia). Its niche is long-duration and seasonal storage.

thermal

Molten salt (CSP)

A nitrate salt mixture is heated by the sun from about 290 °C to 565 °C and kept in a hot tank; at night it raises steam for the turbine. Typical Spanish plants store 7.5 hours; Gemasolar stores 15. See CSP.

thermal

Hot-water tanks and pits

From a domestic solar tank to huge insulated pits that store summer solar heat for winter district heating. Water is cheap and holds a lot of heat. See Solar thermal.

thermal

Industrial heat stores

Hot rocks, sand, ceramic bricks or phase-change materials charged with cheap electricity or waste heat, delivering steam or hot air to industrial processes.

5 · Europe and Spain

Where storage stands

Europe installed 36 GWh of batteries in 2025, 48% more than in 2024, and its fleet passed 100 GWh; for the first time, more than half went to utility-scale projects. Germany, the UK and Italy were the largest markets. SolarPower Europe expects the EU fleet to reach about 470 GWh by 2030.

Spain relies mostly on pumped hydro (3.3 GW). Grid batteries were almost absent until recently: Red Eléctrica counted 28 MW a year before May 2026 and 193 MW then, a jump driven by the lessons of the 2025 blackout. Spain also holds one of the world's largest thermal stores: its CSP fleet of about 20 plants with 7.5 hours of molten salt can store on the order of 7 GWh of electricity (derived: ≈20 × 50 MW × 7.5 h).
